Japan’s five sign groups—regulatory, warning, guide, instruction, and supplementary—with meanings and driver actions for common exam topics. MenkyoNavi is not a government agency.
Shape, color, and text each have a role. Learn the five classifications first, and always read primary signs together with supplementary plates.

Japanese road signs are grouped into guide, warning, regulatory, instruction, and supplementary types. Written exams test what you should do in a situation—not picture memorization alone. This library summarizes definitions you can verify in National Police Agency and MLIT public materials. We do not state specific penalties or fine amounts here; rely on the latest official sources.

Color and shape hint at the sign group. Knowing the group helps you infer required action even for unfamiliar signs.
Show destinations, distances, and facilities to help you choose a route.

Guide signs generally do not create a direct legal duty or prohibition. Examples include direction/distance panels and expressway guidance. When you follow guide information, still check regulatory signs, instruction signs, and signals.
Alert you to hazards or road changes ahead so you can adjust early.

The typical shape is a yellow diamond with a black symbol. They announce places where you should adjust speed and sightlines—curves, railroad crossings, schools, crosswalks, and more. A warning sign alone does not always require a full stop, but you may need to slow down or stop depending on conditions.
State what you must not do, must do, or may do.

Red-ring circles often prohibit; blue circles may prescribe (for example minimum speed). This group ties closely to the Road Traffic Act—full stop, no entry, speed limits, no parking, and similar rules are easier to organize for study in this category.
Tell you mandatory routes or how to use the road.

Often blue rectangles with white arrows or text—one-way direction, lane use, pedestrians only, and similar “proceed this way” orders. Do not confuse them with circular regulatory signs; learn shape together with meaning.
Add time, distance, or vehicle-type limits to a primary sign.

Never drive from a supplementary plate alone. Always read it with the primary sign above or beside it—regulatory, warning, or instruction. Distance/area, day/time, and vehicle-type plates are typical examples of how the same rule applies only in a defined scope.
Do not read supplementary plates alone
If “no parking” has a time plate underneath, the rule is defined by the primary sign plus the plate. Do not assume “free to park” from a white plate by itself.

The same sign type may appear at intersections, roadside, or overhead. Here is what to check first in each situation.

Japan’s “Tomare” (止まれ) sign is an inverted red triangle—not the U.S. octagonal STOP. Stop completely immediately before the stop line (or before the intersection if there is no line), look, then proceed when safe. Slowing down is not enough.
Full stop before the line → look → go when safe
A red circle with a white bar prohibits vehicle entry from your direction. Confirm flow direction so you do not confuse it with a one-way entrance.
Do not enter from the prohibited direction; choose another route
The number is the upper speed limit in km/h for that section. Safe driving often means staying below the limit in rain, darkness, or heavy traffic. Check separate signs where minimum speed applies.
The limit is a ceiling, not a target speed
No parking restricts longer parking; no stopping restricts both brief stops and parking. Time and vehicle-type plates often refine the rule—read them with the primary sign.
Primary sign + supplementary plate = when and for whom
Crosswalk warnings announce pedestrian crossing areas. School/nursery warnings remind you that children may appear. Regardless of signs, study rules that protect pedestrians already crossing.
Sign warns you → reduce speed and watch pedestrians
Diamond warnings are hazard previews—railroads, merges, surface conditions, and more. Adjust mirrors, speed, and following distance early; slow down or stop if needed.
Preview → adjust speed → stop if necessary
A supplementary plate alone tells me the rule
Supplementary plates modify a primary sign. Read them together; never decide from a white plate alone.
Every warning sign means I must make a full stop
Full stops are mainly where regulatory full-stop signs (or equivalent control) apply. Warnings focus on caution and speed adjustment.
Maximum speed 40 means I should drive exactly 40 km/h
It is an upper limit. Often a lower speed is appropriate for weather, visibility, or traffic.
Guides inform route choice. Legal orders come from regulatory/instruction signs and signals—check those when following a guide.
Slowing down replaces a full stop
Where a full stop is designated, you must stop completely before checking and going.

You approach a stop line where a full stop is required. What must you do first?
Slow down and roll through while looking left and right
Stop completely before the stop line, then check left, right, and ahead
Enter the intersection if no car is behind you
Proceed without stopping if no oncoming traffic
A designated full stop means zero speed at the line, then look, then go without obstructing cross traffic.
You see a no-entry sign facing your direction of travel. What is appropriate?
Do not enter with your vehicle from that direction
Enter if no pedestrians are present
No entry prohibits vehicle entry from that direction—choose another route.
Which understanding of a maximum speed 40 sign is correct for study?
You must not drive below 40 km/h
You must not exceed 40 km/h—it is an upper limit
40 km/h is always safe in rain
Maximum speed is a ceiling; slower speeds may be appropriate for conditions.
No parking with a day/time supplementary plate underneath—how should you read it?
Combine the primary sign with the time conditions on the plate
Parking is banned at all times
Supplementary plates limit or extend the primary sign; both define the rule.
A “slow down” (slow speed) sign most closely requires which approach?
Always stop completely at the stop line
Proceed at a speed from which you can stop immediately if needed
Match the speed of traffic behind you
Slow speed (徐行) is not always a full stop, but you must be able to stop right away.
What does a one-way instruction sign indicate?
You may enter from either direction
You may use the opposite lane to pass
One-way signs prescribe the permitted direction of travel.
After seeing a railroad crossing ahead warning, what attitude is closest to correct?
Approach at a speed where you can stop; check trains and gates
Speed up because the warning passed
At crossings, control speed and watch gates, signals, and trains.
Where can I confirm official Japanese sign names?
This page uses learner-friendly titles; official names are shown via site configuration and in NPA/MLIT road-sign references. Exams may test official names and shapes.
Is Japan’s full-stop sign the same as U.S. STOP?
The role is similar, but shape and wording differ. Japan uses an inverted red triangle with “Tomare” (止まれ). Do not rely on foreign sign habits alone.
What if a sign is hard to see?
Reduce speed and use pavement markings, signals, and traffic behavior—not just the sign face. Choose the safer option when unsure.

Where a full stop is designated at an uncontrolled intersection or similar location, you must stop immediately before the stop line (or before the intersection if there is no line). The sign is an inverted red triangle displaying “Tomare” (止まれ).
Full stop before the line → check left, right, ahead, and blind spots → proceed without obstructing others.
Poor visibility at a “Tomare” intersection: stop at the line, verify zero speed, including for cyclists from the left.
Thinking rolling slow or crawl satisfies the rule.
Educational diagram of Japan’s inverted-triangle full-stop sign
Vehicles must not enter from the sign’s direction.
A red circle with a white horizontal bar prohibits vehicle entry from that direction—often at one-way entrances or wrong-way prevention points.
Do not enter from the barred direction; reroute safely.
Alley entrance shows no entry—follow local signs over GPS.
Brief entry is OK if you U-turn immediately.
You must not exceed the number shown (km/h).
A circular regulatory sign shows the upper speed limit in km/h for that section—for example, 40 means you must not drive above 40 km/h there.
Stay at or below the limit; reduce further in rain, darkness, congestion, or poor visibility.
Near schools at limit 40—choose a lower speed when children are hard to see.
Treating the number as the speed you “should” always drive.
Parking (extended stopping) is prohibited in the marked area.
Typically a blue circle regulatory sign with red slash marks zones where parking is forbidden; time and vehicle-type plates may refine the rule.
Do not park in the zone; if you must stop briefly, confirm markings and other controls.
Shopping street no parking—check a time plate such as “7:00–9:00”.
Both brief stops and parking are prohibited.
A blue circle with red × prohibits stopping (even briefly) and parking—common near intersections and fire access.
Do not stop within the zone; pick-up/drop-off outside the controlled area.
Near an intersection—taxi stop must be outside the no-stopping zone.
Assuming it is the same as no parking only.
Proceed at a speed from which you can stop immediately.
The inverted-triangle “slow speed” regulatory sign requires travel slow enough to stop at once if needed—not always a full stop, but much slower than normal cruise.
Use slow speed at poor sightlines, before crossings, and wherever children or merges may appear.
Blind crossroads with slow-speed sign—creep, look both ways, then pass if clear.
Equating slow speed with full stop every time.
Vehicles may travel only in the direction shown.
Blue rectangular instruction signs show permitted travel direction with arrows; wrong-way entry may be blocked by separate no-entry signs.
Follow the arrow; confirm sign orientation before entering.
Entering a downtown one-way—check instruction and no-entry at the mouth.
Using the opposite lane to pass oncoming traffic.
All vehicles are prohibited from passing.
Regulatory sign with vehicle symbol and slash closes the road to vehicles (subject to stated exceptions)—pedestrian zones, work zones, etc.
Pedestrian mall entrance—check bicycle rules on separate signs.
Thinking mopeds or kei cars are always exempt.

Yellow diamond warning that a crossing is ahead—approach ready to stop for trains, gates, and alarms.
Slow to a stoppable speed; never enter when gates are down or a train is approaching.
Lead car slows at crossing—do not tailgate; watch gates and both sides.
Accelerating after seeing only the warning sign.
Expect children near schools or nurseries.
Diamond warning for facilities where children may enter the roadway; speed limit signs may appear together.
Reduce speed; watch curbs and parked cars for children.
School commute hours—assume a child may step from behind a parked car.
An intersection where roads cross is near.
Diamond warning for crossing roads—priority still depends on signals, full-stop signs, priority road designation, and width, not this sign alone.
Slow down; scan shape, signals, markings, and cross traffic.
Approach a crossroads—check for stop lines and Tomare signs.
Diamond warning before crosswalks—prepare to yield to pedestrians.
Slow down; look for people about to cross; stop if needed.
Night glare from oncoming headlights—still verify pedestrians at walking speed.
No sign means no duty to pedestrians (statute still applies).
This road has priority at intersections ahead.
Yellow diamond guide sign indicating priority road status—you must not obstruct traffic on that priority road.
If you are on a non-priority approach, slow and yield to priority-road traffic.
Side street merging to an arterial—confirm cross traffic on the priority road.
Priority road means you may always speed up.

Limits which vehicle classes the primary sign targets.
